Q: Can I develop a progressive web application (PWA) using React Native? A:

You can make a React Native application to work similar to PWA if you are focusing datas. There are some options to make easy mobile-server sync applications even in offline.

  • Google Cloud Firestore
  • MongoDB Stitch
  • Pusher

Or you can custom by yourself using AsyncStorage based on a key-value dictionary.

But some functions between Web and mobile apps are different, especially in storage ways, background process and service worker. Thus, the react libraries related in PWA may not work in React Native, because there isn’t any service worker and local storage is different.

Q: How to avoid the partial function Map.lookup, when the key is known to be in the map? A:

How about handling all the duplicates at once?

replace :: [(Char, Int)] -> [(Char, Foo)]
replace [] = []
replace x@((c, i):cis) = [(c', replacement) | (c', _) <- sameI] ++ replace diffI
    where
    (sameI, diffI) = partition (\(_, i') -> i == i') x
    replacement = Foo . sum . map snd $ cis

This will compute different replacements than yours with the sum way of choosing a replacement, but perhaps in your situation the choice is more robust to deleting subcomponents in the recursive step.

> replace [('a',3), ('c',20), ('d',7), ('d',3), ('a',20)]
[('a',Foo 50),('d',Foo 50),('c',Foo 27),('a',Foo 27),('d',Foo 0)]
-- ('a',3)    ('d',3)      ('c',20)     ('a',20)     ('d',7)

Unfortunately this way, though concise, has worse asymptotics. This can be fixed by splitting into three lists instead of just two and binary searching. I didn't start with that because it's enough more complicated that I think it's hiding the key idea. But here's how that would look:

splitOn :: Ord b => (a -> b) -> b -> [a] -> ([a], [a], [a])
splitOn f pivot = go where
    go [] = ([], [], [])
    go (a:as) = let (lt, eq, gt) = go as in case compare (f a) pivot of
        LT -> (a:lt, eq, gt)
        EQ -> (lt, a:eq, gt)
        GT -> (lt, eq, a:gt)

replace :: [(Char, Int)] -> [(Char, Foo)]
replace [] = []
replace other = go (minimum (snd <$> other)) (maximum (snd <$> other)) other where
    go lo hi [] = []
    go lo hi cis = result where
        med = (lo + hi) `div` 2
        (lt, eq, gt) = splitOn snd med cis
        replacement = Foo . sum . map snd $ cis
        result = []
            ++ go lo (med-1) lt
            ++ [(c', replacement) | (c', _) <- eq]
            ++ go (med+1) hi gt

Q: Applying a git post-commit hook to all current and future repositories A:

This is what I did on my laptop:

  1. Instruct Git to run pre-commit hook from ~/.githooks, as suggested earlier:
git config --global core.hooksPath ~/.githooks
  1. Create an executable pre-commit file over there (need to have pre-commit installed):
#!/bin/bash
set -ex
pre-commit run --config ~/.githooks/config.yaml
  1. Create ~/.githooks/config.yaml for pre-commit (just an example, my actual config file is larger than this one):
repos:
-   repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v5.0.0
    hooks:
    -   id: check-added-large-files
    -   id: check-toml
    -   id: check-xml
    -   id: check-yaml
    -   id: trailing-whitespace

Now, in all my Git repositories the hook works (no need to configure each and every repository).

Q: When should I use a project reference as opposed to a binary reference? A:

I tend to treat common libraries like this as 3rd-party resources. This allows the library to have it's own build processes, QA testing, etc. When QA (or whomever) "blesses" a release of the library, it's copied to a central location available to all developers. It's then up to each project to decide which version of the library to consume by copying the binaries to a project folder and using binary references in the projects.

One thing that is important is to create debug symbol (pdb) files with each build of the library and make those available as well. The other option is to actually create a local symbol store on your network and have each developer add that symbol store to their VS configuration. This would allow you to debug through the code and still have the benefits of usinng binary references.

As for the benefits you mention for project references, I don't agree with your second point. To me, it's important that the consuming projects explicitly know which version of the common library they are consuming and for them to take a deliberate step to upgrade that version. This is the best way to guarantee that you don't accidentally pick up changes to the library that haven't been completed or tested.

Q: git add, commit and push commands in one? A:

This will add all files, add commit message and push code in branch_name

git commit -am "message"; git push origin branch_name
